rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The retention pattern will guide gradient-window trimming and targeted slope or temperature changes.
Double the gradient duration with the window and temperature unchanged to identify slope-responsive coelutions. The first run leaves ample time for a shallower diagnostic gradient.
Keep the successful shallower gradient and raise temperature to test selectivity of the remaining close pair. Higher temperature should also create time margin for further resolution optimization.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 60 C to improve the remaining R = 1.10 pair while retaining the favorable temperature selectivity. The last peak at 8.56 minutes leaves room for this change without a time penalty.

The remaining close pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so shorten tG to move it away from coelution. This should improve that pair and shorten the run; the earlier R = 1.61 pair will be checked for any loss of resolution.

The 18-minute gradient is nearly fully resolved, so test a small temperature adjustment to separate the R = 1.46 pair. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature selectivity, with ample margin below the 10-minute cutoff.

Return to 60 C and shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 5's slope. This tests whether a modest starting-composition change can resolve the marginal pair without sacrificing the other close pairs, while shortening retention.

Use a slope between the recent trials to improve the early close pairs while preserving separation of the later pair. The narrower window ends well above the observed last-peak elution composition, keeping all compounds within the gradient.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to bring the marginal early pairs above R = 1.5. The later close pair has some resolution margin, and the last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Injection 9 reaches the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark while seeking a shorter fully resolved method. Raise the starting organic fraction to advance elution, with a shallower slope to help preserve the early critical separations.

Flatten the gradient modestly at the higher starting fraction to improve the R = 1.08 pair. Monitor the later R = 1.78 pair for a selectivity crossover while testing whether full resolution can be recovered near seven minutes.

Keep injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark and test a substantially different temperature for an alternative selectivity pattern. Holding its gradient fixed isolates the temperature effect and may reveal a route to faster full resolution.

Shorten the low-temperature gradient to test whether its remaining close pair separates with increased slope. This also reduces the 9.62-minute last-peak time; injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score method.

The low-temperature critical pair needs a shallower rather than steeper gradient. Raise the starting fraction while reducing the slope to 0.04 per minute, testing whether improved separation can be combined with earlier elution; retain injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Hold composition and temperature fixed and flatten the gradient to separate the coeluting middle pair. The 6.84-minute last peak leaves room to gain resolution without necessarily exceeding the 10-minute scoring cutoff.

The critical pair improved from R = 0.00 to 1.11 as tG increased from 10 to 14 minutes; extend by one more grid step to target full resolution. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially establishing a second maximum-score method.
Raise temperature by one step from the fully resolved low-temperature method to shorten retention. Keeping the gradient fixed will show whether the critical R = 1.61 pair retains adequate separation.

Test 40 C to move beyond the late-pair convergence seen at 30 C and seek a faster fully resolved selectivity pattern. Injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score benchmark while this alternative temperature region is explored.

Increase temperature one step to test whether the middle-cluster crossover at 40 C opens into adequate separation. This preserves the gradient for a clean selectivity comparison and could shorten elution beyond the current fully resolved benchmark.

Test a shallower gradient at 45 C to improve the three marginal pairs, using the substantial time margin from the 6.72-minute last peak. Keep injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark while checking this potentially faster selectivity region.

Return to the successful 60 C selectivity and test a higher starting fraction with a compensating shallower gradient. This explores a shorter fully resolved method while retaining injection 9 as the proven maximum-score choice.

Test the steep-gradient side of the middle-pair crossover seen at this starting composition, aiming for a substantially faster alternative. Use 30 C to shift the late-pair selectivity, while retaining injection 9 as the established maximum-score method.

Steepen the promising short gradient to move the remaining close pair farther from its crossover and reduce retention further. Monitor the neighboring R = 1.81 pair for compression; injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score fallback.

Lower temperature one step to test whether selectivity can rescue the compressed middle cluster in the fastest trial. Check the late pair carefully for loss of separation, while retaining injection 9 as the established maximum-score method.

For the final trial, shift injection 22's window upward at unchanged slope to test whether starting-composition selectivity resolves its lone R = 0.99 pair while shortening retention. Retain injection 9 as the proven CRF = 1.000 method if this faster candidate falls short.
